flashcards.q: What are the two independent axes in the ECS/EKS/Fargate/EC2 decision?
flashcards.a: Orchestrator (ECS = AWS-native scheduling API, EKS = full Kubernetes API) and compute engine (Fargate = serverless, no node management, EC2 = you manage the fleet). Any combination of the two is valid: ECS+Fargate, ECS+EC2, EKS+Fargate, EKS+EC2.

flashcards.q: Does Fargate support GPU workloads, on ECS or EKS?
flashcards.a: No, on neither. Fargate has zero GPU support. Any GPU-dependent workload must use EC2 launch type, on either ECS or EKS.

flashcards.q: Decode the EC2 instance name c6i.2xlarge.
flashcards.a: c = compute-optimized family, 6 = 6th generation, i = Intel processor, 2xlarge = size tier. Trailing option letters like g (Graviton/ARM), n (enhanced networking), d (local NVMe), e (extra memory/storage) can also appear after the generation number.

flashcards.q: Rank EC2 purchase options by typical discount range vs on-demand.
flashcards.a: Spot: up to ~90% (reclaimable, 2-min notice). EC2 Instance Savings Plans and Standard Reserved Instances: up to ~72% (locked to instance family). Compute Savings Plans: up to ~66% but most flexible, covering EC2, Fargate, and Lambda under one commitment.

flashcards.q: What's the control-plane cost difference between ECS and EKS?
flashcards.a: ECS control plane is $0. EKS control plane costs roughly $0.10/hour per cluster, about $73/month, before any workload compute cost.

flashcards.q: What is AWS's pragmatic default recommendation for a new AWS-only project's compute in 2026, and when should you deviate?
flashcards.a: ECS on Fargate is the default: zero control-plane fee, minimal ops, fast to stand up. Deviate to EKS only for a concrete trigger -- multi-cloud/hybrid strategy, a Kubernetes-native tool dependency, or an existing platform team already fluent in kubectl serving many internal tenants.

flashcards.q: What's the maximum size of a single AWS Batch array job, and what workload shape is it built for?
flashcards.a: Up to 10,000 child jobs from one submission. Built for embarrassingly parallel work -- same code, many independent inputs, no coordination between units (Monte Carlo sweeps, parametric jobs, bulk file transforms). Wrong tool for anything needing inter-task communication or ordering.

flashcards.q: What is a warm pool in an Auto Scaling Group, and why does it exist alongside normal ASG scaling?
flashcards.a: A pool of pre-initialized instances kept in Stopped (storage-cost only) or Running state alongside the ASG. It exists because plain ASG scale-out boots cold from the AMI and can take minutes for slow-bootstrapping workloads; pulling from a warm pool instead cuts scale-out latency to seconds.

flashcards.q: What do ASG lifecycle hooks do, and what problem do they solve?
flashcards.a: They pause an instance in a Pending:Wait or Terminating:Wait state so custom automation (config pull, log flush, connection draining) can run before the instance is marked in-service or actually terminated. Without them, ASG considers an instance ready the moment EC2 reports it running, often before the application has finished bootstrapping.

flashcards.q: Distinguish the Spot interruption notice from the rebalance recommendation.
flashcards.a: The interruption notice is a hard, fixed 2-minute warning before AWS reclaims the instance. The rebalance recommendation is a separate, earlier signal indicating elevated risk of interruption, commonly with more lead time in practice but not a guaranteed fixed window -- meant to let you proactively move workload before the hard 2-minute notice arrives.

flashcards.q: What does Nitro do, and why do current-generation EC2 instances get near-bare-metal performance?
flashcards.a: Nitro is the underlying hypervisor/hardware architecture on current-generation instances that offloads virtualization overhead (networking, storage) to dedicated hardware, reducing hypervisor tax versus the older Xen-based architecture and enabling finer-grained instance sizing.

flashcards.q: What are the three EC2 placement group types and their use cases?
flashcards.a: Cluster: instances packed physically close for low-latency, high-throughput networking (HPC, tightly-coupled distributed training). Spread: each instance on distinct hardware, for a small number of critical instances that must not share a failure domain. Partition: groups spread across logical, isolated failure domains, for partition-aware distributed systems like HDFS or Cassandra.

flashcards.q: Why do Reserved Instances lock in more risk than Savings Plans despite similar discount ranges?
flashcards.a: Standard Reserved Instances lock to a specific instance family for the 1-3 year term (can modify AZ/size within family, not the family itself), whereas Compute Savings Plans apply flexibly across instance family, region, and even compute type (EC2, Fargate, Lambda) under one dollar-per-hour commitment.
